name: Fragrance wheel

lead: The fragrance wheel is a circular diagram that groups perfumes into families, with similar-smelling families placed next to each other. It helps your appearance and presence by making it easier to pick a scent that fits you, since fragrance is part of overall grooming.

The best-known version was devised by perfume taxonomist Michael Edwards. Shoppers and retailers use it to move from a scent they already like to neighbouring families, while perfumers use it to see which families blend well.

paras: A common approach is to find the family of a fragrance you already like, then try perfumes in the neighbouring segments. Fresh families (citrus, aromatic, water) sit opposite warm amber ones, with floral and woody families on the other axis. Fragrance sellers and brand quizzes often organise recommendations by these families, and people also use them to match scent to season or occasion.

The wheel has no safety implications itself. Fragrance products can cause skin irritation or allergy in some people. The wheel's categories overlap, and critics note that associating families with gender can limit choices.

angle.text: The wheel does not change appearance directly. It organises scents so people can choose a fragrance for their grooming routine more deliberately.

lead: The fragrance wheel is a circular classification chart for perfumes. Related scent families are placed next to one another, so the diagram shows which odours are alike and which sit opposite [1]. Edwards designed his version to help retailers and consumers navigate the market [1].

For anyone working on grooming and style, the chart serves as a map for choosing a signature scent: start from a known favourite, then explore adjacent segments. Perfumers use the same map to pair notes from compatible families [2].
The first wheel-style diagram, Paul Jellinek's Odor Effects Diagram, appeared in 1949 according to Wikipedia, and Michael Edwards introduced his widely used Fragrance Wheel in 1992 [1].

paras: In Edwards's 2010 layout the main families are Floral, Amber, Woody and Fresh, each divided into subfamilies: Soft Floral and Floral Amber; Soft Amber and Woody Amber; Woods, Mossy Woods and Dry Woods; and Aromatic, Citrus, Water, Green and Fruity [1]. Some scents, such as Chanel No. 5, fit more than one group [1].
Another description of the wheel places Floral at the top, Amber at the right, Woody at the bottom and Fresh on the left, with bridges linking neighbouring families [2].

Besides Jellinek (1949) and Edwards (1992), Wikipedia lists U. Harder's Fragrance Circle (1979) and Ann Noble's Wine Aroma Wheel (1984) as other circular scent diagrams [1]. Edwards's original 1983 layout had Fougère at its centre and an Oriental family; in 2008 he added Woods and Fruity subgroups, and in 2010 Amber largely replaced Oriental and Aromatics moved on the wheel [1]. Grokipedia gives differing dates for the first edition and mentions later renaming of Oriental to Ambery [2].

Shoppers use the wheel to find what they like and to choose by season, and brands use family-based quizzes to recommend products [2]. Critics note that marketing has long tied Floral to women and Woody to men, which can narrow self-expression [2]. The diagram also struggles with niche perfumes that span several families [2].
No studies found. A 2026 plant-science paper uses the term for floral scent types in Hedychium flowers, a different application [3].
